fatal_errors: The proposed intervention omits the high-energy ball milling and spark-plasma-sintering route central to the target.

The mechanism is opposite to the target: it claims Ti-induced lattice distortion facilitates glide, whereas the target attributes strengthening to nanocrystalline grain boundaries, milling-induced dislocation density, solid-solution strengthening, densification, and an FCC/BCC phase mixture.

The baseline changes composition to CoCrFeNi rather than comparing against conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi, confounding Ti content with phase stability, stacking-fault energy, and other deformation variables.
The predicted reduction in hardness and strength conflicts with the reported approximately 675 Hv hardness, 1238 MPa yield stress, and 1894 MPa compressive strength after milling and SPS.

Neither cited source provides direct evidence that Ti lowers dislocation-motion barriers in CoCrFeNiTi; one concerns CrCoNi twin boundaries and the other merely describes dislocation characterization in unrelated refractory alloys.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses deformation and offers a nominally testable TEM/mechanical comparison, but it does not reconstruct the material-processing hypothesis or reported results. It misses the 1–6 h, 400 rpm milling treatment, 20:1 ball-to-powder ratio, 900–1000 °C SPS window, nanocrystalline grain refinement, densification, and 83% FCC/17% BCC structure. Its composition-changing baseline cannot uniquely attribute behavior to Ti-induced local distortion, and thin-foil TEM mobility may not represent bulk deformation. Although the stated single-phase, room-temperature loading boundary and falsification measurements are useful, the proposed causal mechanism lacks relevant evidence and is contradicted by the target's strengthening mechanism and outcomes.
